historical_record.description: The Green family planted the eucalyptus, pines and ferns that still grow in the grove, and George W. Green planted Holland grass to hold the sandy slopes.

George W. Green, son of the Green family who had farmed the ravine since the 1840s, built the Trocadero Inn, a two-story Stick-Eastlake roadhouse and inn on his family's land; its architect and builder are unknown.

Earnest Doelter was running the Trocadero Inn, the first of a string of proprietors that went on to include lumberman C. A. Hooper and boxing referee Hiram Cook, who added a dance pavilion, beer garden, deer park, trout pond and weekend cabins.
Businessman Adolph Spreckels leased the inn for a short time.
On William H. Green's death the heavily mortgaged family farm, including the Trocadero, passed to his son George W. Green.
Political boss Abe Ruef, indicted in the San Francisco graft trials, hid at the Trocadero and was captured there by detectives, a front-page story.
Proprietor J. N. Soldanels advertised the Trocadero as an ideal family resort serving meals all night.
After the proprietor gave up his lease, George W. Green offered the building and nineteen acres around it for sale but found no buyer.

The newly formed Woman's Outdoor Club, led by Mabel Hawkins (Mrs. Charles Hawkins), took the Trocadero as its clubhouse, offering members overnight stays, dances, picnics, cooking and folklore classes and open-air theatricals.
The Woman's Outdoor Club held a Jubilee Picnic of suffragists here to celebrate passage of California's Proposition 4, which gave women the vote in the state.
The Girl Pioneers of America ran a summer camp in the valley around the Trocadero, with tents, strawberry picking and long hikes.
The Woman's Outdoor Club's weekly Sunday dances at the Trocadero drew objections from the public and the Board of Supervisors.
The Sanborn map showed the Trocadero as a dwelling with the same footprint it has today, among a small dwelling, wagon shed, rabbit pens and greenhouse in the wooded ravine.
George W. Green closed the Trocadero as a roadhouse.
The building's brief run as the Ardenglen Country Club ended when it was refused a liquor license.

Rosalie Meyer Stern bought the Trocadero Inn and twelve acres around it for $50,000 through the Sigmund Stern Recreational Fund, set up in memory of her husband, and gave them to the city for recreational use only.
Age and debts forced George W. Green, who had built the Trocadero and lived in it tending the grounds, to sell the property; he died in 1934.
Bernard Maybeck restored and repaired the old inn for park use, leaving it largely as it was; he called it perfect as he found it.
Sigmund Stern Recreation Grove was dedicated, and the old inn became the Trocadero Clubhouse, rented out for parties and club meetings.
The first concert was held in the Stern Grove amphitheater.
WPA workers began building stone retaining walls, gutters and steps up toward 21st Avenue, stone barbecues, and a fish pond with paths around the clubhouse, finishing in 1937.
The Historic American Buildings Survey photographed the clubhouse; measured drawings followed in 1937.
The grove's annual Midsummer Music Festival began.
The Ladies' Convenience Station was built directly beside the clubhouse, joined to it by the porch.
With the new Wawona Clubhouse built nearby, the Trocadero stopped serving as the park's clubhouse and became an event space.
A fire damaged the second floor, likely prompting interior alterations.
The building was documented in Here Today: San Francisco's Architectural Heritage.
The building was being used for administrative offices.
The building was rated 2 in the Department of City Planning's architectural quality survey.

A Page & Turnbull renovation undid the 1950s–60s interior changes and returned the building to its 1930s appearance, with seismic stabilization, disabled access, restored ornament and finishes, and new stained-glass windows by Kimiko Kogure matching the historic look.

Work was approved to add ground-floor restrooms, renovate floors and walls, upgrade electrics, replace the fireplace, and replace the wood porch and ramp with a larger deck on the west side for accessibility.
Work was approved to replace the deteriorated wood deck, ramp and guardrails and to rebuild the historic part of the guardrail to its original design from photographs and HABS drawings.
The Board of Supervisors initiated landmark designation of the clubhouse.
The Mayor approved the resolution initiating the clubhouse's landmark designation.
The Historic Preservation Commission recommended the clubhouse's designation as a city landmark.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 301, Trocadero Clubhouse.

unknowns: Maybeck's partner on the restoration is named both as William Merchant and as Gardner Dailey.
